sections.title: Structure of a GSL Speech
sections.content: A General Speakers List speech is your first impression in committee. You have 60-90 seconds to state your country's position. The optimal structure: Hook + Stance + Policy + Call to Action.
bullets: Hook — Open with a compelling fact, quote, or question
Stance — Clearly state your country's position on the topic
Policy — Outline 1-2 specific policy solutions your country supports
Call to Action — End with what you want the committee to do

sections.title: What to Avoid
sections.content: Many delegates waste their GSL by reading from a paper, speaking too fast, or being too vague. Your GSL should sound natural and conversational even though it is prepared.
bullets: Do not read word-for-word from a script
Do not try to cover every aspect of the topic
Do not use jargon without explanation
Do make eye contact with the chair and other delegates

sections.instruction: What is the first element of a strong GSL speech?
sections.feedback: Start with a hook — a compelling fact, quote, or question that makes the committee want to listen.

sections.q: Why should you avoid reading your GSL speech word-for-word?
options: It sounds robotic and reduces your perceived confidence
sections.explain: Reading sounds unprepared and reduces eye contact. Know your key points and speak naturally.

sections.statement: A GSL speech should cover every aspect of the committee topic in detail.
sections.feedback: A GSL is a broad overview, not a detailed analysis. Focus on 1-2 key points.

sections.sentence: The four elements of a GSL speech are: Hook, {0}, Policy, and Call to Action.
sections.feedback: Hook → Stance → Policy → Call to Action

sections.instruction: Double-click or tap each card to place it in the correct section of the GSL speech.

cards.text: "Every 39 seconds, a cyberattack happens somewhere in the world."
"Japan believes that cybersecurity is a shared responsibility requiring international cooperation."
"We propose a global cyber-incident reporting framework based on the Budapest Convention model."
"I urge every delegate here to co-sponsor our working paper on cross-border cyber cooperation."

sections.feedback: Great job! A strong GSL speech flows: Hook → Stance → Policy → Call to Action.

questions.instruction: Put the four GSL speech elements in order.
questions.feedback: Hook attracts attention, Stance states your position, Policy offers solutions, Call to Action drives action.
